newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Trends, deceptions and porkies -- polling in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Trends, deceptions and porkies -- polling in NZ.

text.p: Prime Minister Jim Bolger echoed the thoughts of many New Zealanders when on election night in 1993 he said: "Bugger the pollsters".
As with other recent notable failures in Britain, Canada and Australia, polls got New Zealand's last election result wrong by showing the National Party leading by up to 10 points.
In fact, on election night it was a hung parliament, with National finally winning by the barest of majorities.
Pollsters, politicians and political scientists say polls are useful to identify trends and as a rough snapshot.
So what are the trends apparent just five weeks ahead of New Zealand first mixed proportion election on October 12?
National's support has been consistent around 35-40 percent, said Canterbury University political scientist Keith Jackson, while support has been swapping among opposition parties.
A political lobbyist, who declined to be named, said the major change in the last year had been reallocation of support on the left, with no real change in the size of the total opposition.
National's long-term trend had started to look a bit weak, in the past fortnight, he said.
Auckland University political scientist Helena Catt said the idea that National is going down, and the recent revival of the left-of-centre Labour Party, was the most realistic message.
She said volatility in support for economic nationalist New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance showed they did not have solid, stable, loyal support.
"It means the election campaign could have a big impact on both of those parties depending on how voters react to what they are doing," she said.

National Party strategist Richard Griffin said its polling showed National "looking pretty sick in terms of trends two months ago but in the last month, things have improved a good deal." It showed no major upturn in the Alliance's vote.
Alliance Director Matt McCarten said that party's polls showed the conservative vote up around the 40 percent mark.
"People are just a bit unsure who to back among the other three on the opposition -- that's what the opposition is going to be all about," he said.
Recent gains by the Christian Coalition and free market ACT Party were coming at National's expense, McCarten said.
Since the last election, Labour had never had better than 25 percent support, he said. On the other hand, there was no question NZ First had had a good run "and we got a bit of hit".
NZ First does not poll or even have focus groups. "We go on gut instinct," a spokesman said.
Labour said its polling were in line was public polls although both displayed bias towards National, Deputy Leader Michael Cullen said.
He said half the people polled refuse to cooperate. "If those 50 percent are systematically different from the other 50 percent, you have a major problem with the results.

"We are finding in our samples, after you take out the refusals, that they are systematically biased towards the 1993 National Party voters. Whatever the reason, it sure as hell is influencing the polls quite significantly."
Stephen Mills of UMR-Insight, which polls for the National Business Review, defends the accuracy of polls, saying differences usually occur because of timing gaps between polling and publication.
He said their poll and others showed National losing steadily in the last couple of weeks before the 1993 election.
"Overall, I don't think the picture was that disastrous," he said. "It's the ones taken late that prove to be right."
Brownwyn Fisher of Colmar-Brunton, pollster for TV1, said polls are reliable if placed in context.
"They are very reliable but we have to remember that they are a measure of how people are feeling today rather than how people are going to vote on election day."
While polls are highlighted by news media because they constantly change and can be billed as exclusives, political scientists point to other shortcomings.

"One of the things that is worrying is they are not really reporting the undecided/don't knows, which is often around 20 percent, and from what we know of the last election it can remain up there up until the last couple of days," said Catt.
"So unless a party is over 20 percent ahead, everything could change when those 20 percent of people decide to vote.

Jackson said the margin of error for some polls is over three percent and for TV3 with a sample of just 500 it is even greater. The polls may not fully account for the new mixed proportional system and the novelty of two votes, said Jackson.
Mills admits this is uncharted territory.

"It's another source of volatility. It's hard to know because we have not been in it before. My impression is people have a very limited appreciation of the mechanics of MMP (mixed member proportional) and that could well feed in to poll answers as well as their final voting choices."
Catt said polls trends may influence how people will vote, particularly for small parties, and for this reason are banned in some countries in the lead up to elections.

If a poll showed a party nearing the five percent threshold needed to win proportional seats, there would be a huge push to get over the threshold. Conversely a party polling poorly may influence people not to "waste" their vote for that party.
"In some electorates a poll showing who are the top two contenders may galvanise support or opposition," Catt said.
However, banning could open the door for companies to make big money by commissioning their own polls.
